questions.question:
ShopFlow's finance team runs a month-end revenue report directly against the production Postgres database. On the last day of each month, customers complain that checkout is slow while the report runs. The report must still be refreshed daily, and checkout performance must not be affected.

What should you do?

options.text: Add more indexes to the `orders` table so the report runs faster
Copy the order data into the lakehouse on a schedule and run the report there
Run the report at 2 am so fewer customers are affected
Give the finance team a read-only user on the production database

questions.explanation:
**Why B is right:** Production Postgres is an **OLTP** system, built for many tiny reads and writes. A big analytical scan competes with customers' transactions and is slow itself, because the database is laid out for small transactions, not big scans. Moving the data into a separate **OLAP** system (the lakehouse) is exactly why data engineering exists: analytics without breaking the business.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — The heavy scan still runs on the live database and competes with checkout; the course's answer is to move analytics off the OLTP system, not to tune it.
- **C** — It only moves the problem to another hour; the heavy query still hits production, and the report must be refreshed daily anyway.
- **D** — Read-only access doesn't make the scan lighter; it still runs on the production database.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › OLTP vs OLAP

questions.question:
ShopFlow wants to keep an untouched copy of everything it receives, and to use the lakehouse's own compute to clean and aggregate the data afterwards, in successive layers.

Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: ETL — transform on a separate engine, then load the result
ELT — load the raw data first, then transform it in place
OLTP — process many small transactions
Full load — copy every table again each night

questions.explanation:
**Why B is right:** **ELT** loads the raw data first and then transforms it with the lakehouse's own compute, so the raw copy is kept. In the medallion pattern, Bronze *is* the loaded raw zone and Silver and Gold are the transform steps.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — ETL transforms before loading, on a separate engine, and often keeps no raw copy, which fails the first requirement.
- **C** — OLTP is the kind of system that runs the business (the source), not a way of moving and transforming data.
- **D** — A full load is an ingestion choice (copy everything vs only changes); it says nothing about where or when the transform happens.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › ETL vs ELT

questions.question:
An Airflow task that loads yesterday's orders failed halfway and was retried. The `daily_sales` mart now shows some orders twice. The team wants re-runs of any task to be safe from now on.

Which property must the pipeline have?

options.text: Idempotent: re-running it produces the same result, with no duplicates
Incremental: it copies only what changed since the last run
Lineage: it records where each piece of data came from
Streaming: it processes events continuously

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** The course defines a good pipeline as **idempotent**: re-running it produces the same result, with no duplicates. That makes retries and backfills safe.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Incremental loading is about copying less data; a retried incremental load can still insert the same rows twice.
- **C** — Lineage is governance: it records where data came from, but doesn't stop duplicates.
- **D** — Streaming is about speed (continuous processing); it doesn't make re-runs safe.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › 5 · Orchestrate & govern

questions.question:
ShopFlow receives customers from three sources. One calls the key `cust_id`, another `customer`, and a CSV file uses `CustomerID` with no types at all. Analysts need one customer table they can join to orders.

Which transform step addresses this?

options.text: Deduplicate
Conform the schemas onto one shared model
Aggregate and apply business logic
Serve the data through a data mart

questions.explanation:
**Why B is right:** Sources disagree: each has its own schema and naming. **Conforming schemas** maps each source's columns onto **one shared model**, so `cust_id`, `customer` and `CustomerID` all become one `customer_id`.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — Deduplication collapses repeated records into one; it doesn't reconcile different column names across sources.
- **C** — Aggregation rolls rows up into metrics; the columns must be conformed before you can aggregate them reliably.
- **D** — Serving exposes finished data; the conflicting schemas have to be fixed earlier, in the transform.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › 3 · Transform
Foundations › What is Data Engineering › A general data pipeline, end to end

questions.question:
The ShopFlow `orders` table has grown to hundreds of millions of rows. Copying the whole table every night now takes too long. The team needs every insert, update and delete as it happens, read from the database's change log.

Which ingestion method should you use?

options.text: Full load
Batch export to CSV
Change Data Capture (CDC)
Schema-on-read

questions.explanation:
**Why C is right:** **CDC** is a smart form of incremental load: it reads the database's change log to capture every insert, update and delete as it happens.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — A full load copies the entire table every time, which is exactly what has become too slow.
- **B** — A batch export is still a scheduled bulk copy; it doesn't read the change log or capture deletes as they happen.
- **D** — Schema-on-read is about when a lake applies structure to files, not about getting changes out of a database.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › 1 · Ingest

questions.question:
A new engineer suggests transforming ShopFlow's data straight from the source systems, without first landing an untouched copy in a staging (raw) zone.

Which **two** benefits would the team lose? (Choose two.)

options.text: Re-running transforms without fetching from the live source again
An audit trail of exactly what arrived
Faster dashboards for executives
Automatic removal of duplicate rows
Encryption of the data at rest

questions.explanation:
**Why A and B are right:** The landing (raw) zone is an exact, untouched copy of what arrived. Keeping it lets you **reprocess without re-fetching** (never hammering the live source twice) and gives you an **audit trail**.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **C** — Dashboard speed comes from Gold marts and serving, not from the raw landing zone.
- **D** — The raw zone deliberately keeps data untouched, duplicates included; deduplication is a transform step.
- **E** — The course doesn't present encryption as a purpose of the staging zone; its purpose is reprocessing and audit.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › 2 · Store
Foundations › What is Data Engineering › A general data pipeline, end to end

questions.question:
ShopFlow needs answers at two speeds. Match each need to the processing speed that fits it.

| Need | Speed |
|---|---|
| Block a fraudulent checkout while it happens | [Fraud check] |
| The trustworthy daily picture of how the business is doing | [Daily picture] |
| Rescue an abandoned cart in the moment | [Abandoned cart] |
questions.explanation:
**Batch** processes data in chunks on a schedule; **streaming** processes events continuously as they arrive.

- **Fraud check → Streaming** — it has to act in the moment, while the checkout happens; a nightly batch would be too late.
- **Daily picture → Batch** — the course describes batch as what builds the daily, trustworthy picture of the business.
- **Abandoned cart → Streaming** — rescuing a cart is acting in the moment, which needs continuous processing.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › Two speeds: batch and streaming

questions.question:
ShopFlow's governance work has four parts. Match each request to the governance discipline that answers it.

| Request | Discipline |
|---|---|
| "Which tables do we have, and what is in them?" | [Request 1] |
| "Where did the numbers in this report come from?" | [Request 2] |
| "Only finance may see the margin table." | [Request 3] |
| "Stop the load if an order has no customer." | [Request 4] |
questions.explanation:
Governance means knowing **what** data you have, **where it came from**, **who may see it** and **whether it's correct**.

- **Request 1 → Catalog** — the catalog is the record of what data you have.
- **Request 2 → Lineage** — lineage records where each piece of data came from.
- **Request 3 → Access control (RBAC)** — access control (RBAC) decides who may see what.
- **Request 4 → Data quality checks** — data quality checks decide whether the data is correct, and can stop a bad load.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › 5 · Orchestrate & govern

questions.question:
ShopFlow is moving its nightly scripts into an orchestrator.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.

slots.label: Orchestration is a stage that runs only at the end of the pipeline.
Pipelines are usually modelled as a DAG of dependent tasks.

questions.explanation:
Orchestration runs the steps in the right **order**, on a **schedule**, with **retries** and **backfills**.

- **Statement 1: No** — orchestration and governance aren't a stage at the end; they run **across** the whole flow.
- **Statement 2: Yes** — the orchestrator runs a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of dependent tasks, in order.
- **Statement 3: Yes** — orchestration includes retries when something fails and backfills to reprocess history.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › 5 · Orchestrate & govern
Foundations › What is Data Engineering › A general data pipeline, end to end

questions.question:
Put the core steps of a ShopFlow pipeline in order, from the source systems to the people who use the data.

1. [Step 1]
2. [Step 2]
3. [Step 3]
4. [Step 4]
questions.explanation:
The data engineer's job follows the same order on every platform; orchestration and governance wrap all of it.

- **Step 1 → Ingest** — first, get data out of the source systems.
- **Step 2 → Store** — land it durably and cheaply (object storage / a lakehouse).
- **Step 3 → Transform** — clean, join and aggregate it into trustworthy shapes.
- **Step 4 → Serve** — expose the finished data to BI, ML and applications.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › The five steps, in depth

questions.question:
ShopFlow's data scientists want clean, ready-made inputs for training and scoring a churn model. Executives already have their dashboards.

Which way of serving data fits the data scientists?

options.text: A feature store
The staging / raw zone
A connector such as JDBC
The OLTP database

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** Serving makes finished data usable for each audience. For ML, the course names **feature stores**: clean features for training and scoring models.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — The raw zone holds untouched data exactly as received; it isn't clean or ready for a model.
- **C** — Connectors are ingestion adapters that read from sources; they don't serve finished data.
- **D** — The OLTP database runs the business; analytics and ML belong on the separate, finished data.

references.title: Foundations › What is Data Engineering › 4 · Serve

questions.question:
ShopFlow wants to keep clickstream JSON, product images and order tables cheaply in open files. It also needs ACID transactions, `MERGE` for late updates, and fast SQL for BI, and data scientists want to read the same raw files.

Which architecture meets all these requirements?

options.text: A classic data warehouse
A plain data lake
A lakehouse
The OLTP database

questions.explanation:
**Why C is right:** A **lakehouse** keeps the lake's cheap, open storage and adds the warehouse's guarantees (ACID, MERGE, time travel, governance) through a table format and a catalog. In the comparison table it is the only option that is good for **both BI and ML**.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — A warehouse is expensive, proprietary, and weak with raw, semi-structured or unstructured data such as JSON and images.
- **B** — A plain lake is cheap and flexible, but has no ACID transactions and makes updates and MERGE hard.
- **D** — The OLTP database runs the business; analytics belongs in a separate OLAP system.

references.title: Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › Lakehouse (the synthesis)
Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › Comparing the three

questions.question:
A company has dumped files into object storage for years. Nobody knows which files are current, there is no schema enforcement, and nobody trusts the numbers.

What has the lake become, and what turns it into a lakehouse?

options.text: A data swamp; add an open table format and a catalog on top of the files
A data swamp; move every file into the OLTP database
A data warehouse; add more storage
A data mart; delete the old files

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** Without discipline a lake rots into a **data swamp**: a pile of files nobody trusts. A **table format** adds ACID and schema enforcement, and a **catalog** adds discovery and access control; together with the storage they make a lakehouse.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — The OLTP database is for running the business, not for analytics over years of files.
- **C** — A pile of untrusted files isn't a warehouse, and more storage doesn't add trust or structure.
- **D** — A data mart is a focused, ready-to-query table for a team; deleting files doesn't make the rest trustworthy.

references.title: Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › Data lake (the reaction)
Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › Lakehouse (the synthesis)

questions.question:
Match each ShopFlow component to the lakehouse layer it provides.

| Component | Layer |
|---|---|
| RustFS holding Parquet files | [RustFS] |
| Iceberg tables | [Iceberg] |
| Apache Polaris | [Polaris] |
questions.explanation:
ShopFlow's lakehouse maps one-to-one onto the three layers.

- **RustFS → Object storage** — S3-compatible object storage: the cheap, open files.
- **Iceberg → Open table format** — the table format that turns the files into real tables.
- **Polaris → Catalog & governance** — the catalog: the namespace, access control (RBAC) and discovery.

references.title: Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › In this course
Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › Lakehouse (the synthesis)

questions.question:
A ShopFlow customer asks for their data to be erased. Their orders are spread across thousands of Parquet files in a plain data lake.

Which lakehouse capability makes this a simple operation?

options.text: Row-level updates and deletes through the table format
Schema-on-read
Columnar compression
Separating storage and compute

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** The table format adds **updates, deletes and MERGE**: changing individual rows for GDPR deletes, corrections or CDC, which is impossible on plain files.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Schema-on-read applies structure when you query; it can't change or remove rows.
- **C** — Compression saves space; it doesn't let you delete a single row.
- **D** — Separating storage and compute is about scaling and paying for each independently, not about changing rows.

references.title: Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › What the table format actually buys you

questions.question:
ShopFlow is comparing the three kinds of analytical storage.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.

slots.label: A plain data lake gives you ACID transactions.
A lakehouse stores its data in open file formats.
A classic data warehouse usually separates storage and compute.

questions.explanation:
These rows come from the course's comparison of warehouse, lake and lakehouse.

- **Statement 1: No** — on its own a lake is just files: no ACID transactions.
- **Statement 2: Yes** — the lakehouse keeps the lake's open files (Parquet) and adds table guarantees on top.
- **Statement 3: No** — classic warehouses **couple** storage and compute, so you pay for both together.

references.title: Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › Comparing the three

questions.question:
Match each storage system to how it applies a schema.

| System | Schema |
|---|---|
| Data warehouse | [Warehouse] |
| Data lake (plain files) | [Lake] |
questions.explanation:
"No schema at all, ever" is wrong for both: a lake still applies structure, only later.

- **Warehouse → Schema-on-write** — data must fit a rigid, pre-defined schema **before** it can be loaded.
- **Lake → Schema-on-read** — files of any shape are stored, and structure is applied only **when you query**.

references.title: Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › Data warehouse (the classic)
Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › Data lake (the reaction)

questions.question:
Last night's load wrote wrong prices into a ShopFlow table, and this morning's Gold report is wrong. You need to see the table exactly as it was before the load.

Which feature do you use?

options.text: Time travel to an earlier version
Schema evolution
Partitioning
Schema-on-read

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** **Time travel** queries a table as it was yesterday or at version N, so you can reproduce a report or roll back a bad load.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Schema evolution safely changes a table's columns over time; it doesn't show earlier data.
- **C** — Partitioning splits a table into folders by a column to read less; it keeps no history.
- **D** — Schema-on-read decides when structure is applied; it can't show the table before the load.

references.title: Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › What the table format actually buys you

questions.question:
ShopFlow analysts can't find the tables they need, and today everyone can read every table. The team wants one `catalog.schema.table` namespace, discovery, and per-table access control.

Which lakehouse layer provides this?

options.text: The catalog (Apache Polaris)
The object storage (RustFS)
The Parquet file format
The query engine (Trino)

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** The **catalog** is the directory of all tables plus governance: a `catalog.schema.table` namespace, access control, discovery and lineage.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Object storage holds the files; it has no table namespace or per-table permissions.
- **C** — Parquet is how one file's bytes are laid out; it knows nothing about other tables or users.
- **D** — Query engines are interchangeable and sit above the catalog; they use its namespace and rules rather than providing them.

references.title: Foundations › Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse › Lakehouse (the synthesis)

questions.question:
A ShopFlow analyst queries a Parquet table with 50 columns, but the query uses only `order_date` and `amount`. The engine physically reads only those two columns.

What is this called?

options.text: Predicate pushdown
Projection pushdown
Partitioning
Compaction (OPTIMIZE)

questions.explanation:
**Why B is right:** **Projection pushdown** reads only the columns a query needs, which works because Parquet is columnar.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — Predicate pushdown skips chunks (row groups) that can't match a **filter**; it is about rows, not columns.
- **C** — Partitioning splits a table into folders by a column value; it doesn't choose which columns are read.
- **D** — Compaction merges many small files into fewer big ones.

references.title: Foundations › File & table formats › The common file formats
Foundations › File & table formats › Row-based vs columnar

questions.question:
A query on ShopFlow's order history filters `WHERE country = 'UK'`. The engine skips whole chunks of each Parquet file without reading them.

What makes this possible?

options.text: Min/max statistics stored per row group
Projection pushdown
Schema-on-read
The OLTP database's indexes

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** Each Parquet chunk (row group) stores **min/max statistics**, so the engine can skip chunks that can't match the filter. This is predicate pushdown, or data skipping.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Projection pushdown skips **columns** the query doesn't use, not chunks of rows.
- **C** — Schema-on-read is about when structure is applied; it doesn't skip any data.
- **D** — The files live in object storage; the source database's indexes play no part in reading them.

references.title: Foundations › File & table formats › The common file formats

questions.question:
ShopFlow stores daily order exports as Parquet files in object storage. Late-arriving updates to existing orders arrive every night and must replace the old rows. Auditors also need to reproduce last Monday's sales report exactly as it was shown.

Which **two** capabilities do you need, which plain Parquet files do not provide? (Choose two.)

options.text: Columnar storage with compression
Row-level `MERGE` / upsert in a single atomic operation
Min/max statistics per row group
Time travel to an earlier table version
A schema embedded in each file

questions.explanation:
**Why B and D are right:** A folder of Parquet files can't change a single row or say what the table looked like last week. A **table format** adds a transaction log that records each version, which gives atomic **MERGE** and **time travel**.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — Parquet is already columnar and compressed; the table format isn't needed for this.
- **C** — Row-group statistics are part of Parquet itself.
- **E** — Parquet files already carry their own schema.

references.title: Foundations › File & table formats › Table formats — turning files into a table

questions.question:
Analysts average the `price` column over 50 million ShopFlow orders, stored as CSV. The query is slow and storage costs are high.

Which **two** reasons explain why converting to Parquet helps? (Choose two.)

options.text: It is columnar, so the query reads only the columns it needs
Similar values sit together, so encodings compress them much better
It is row-based, so each whole record is kept together
It removes the need for a schema
It turns the files into an ACID table

questions.explanation:
**Why A and B are right:** Parquet is **columnar**: the query reads only `price` instead of every column (projection pushdown), and similar values sitting together **compress** far better, which means less storage and less I/O.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **C** — Row-based is CSV's layout; it suits fetching whole records (OLTP), not scanning one column over millions of rows.
- **D** — Parquet is typed and carries its own schema; it doesn't remove the schema.
- **E** — ACID comes from a table format (Delta or Iceberg) on top of Parquet, not from Parquet itself.

references.title: Foundations › File & table formats › Row-based vs columnar
Foundations › File & table formats › The common file formats

questions.question:
ShopFlow partitioned its events table so finely that it now has millions of tiny files, and queries got slower.

What is the problem, and how do you fix it?

options.text: The small-files problem; compact the files with OPTIMIZE
Schema drift; enable schema evolution
Data skew; switch the files to CSV
An orphan key; add an Unknown member

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** Over-partitioning creates the **small-files problem**: millions of tiny files. Compaction (`OPTIMIZE`) merges them into fewer, bigger ones.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Nothing changed in the columns; the problem is the number of files, not the schema.
- **C** — CSV would make reads slower, not faster, and doesn't reduce the number of files.
- **D** — Orphan keys and Unknown members belong to dimensional modeling; they have nothing to do with file counts.

references.title: Foundations › File & table formats › One more term: partitioning

questions.question:
ShopFlow writes its tables from Spark as Delta. Trino must read the same tables as Iceberg, and the team doesn't want to keep two copies of the data.

What should you use?

options.text: Delta with UniForm enabled
Convert every table to CSV
Write a second copy as Iceberg every night
Partition the tables by date

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** **UniForm** publishes Iceberg metadata for the same Delta files, so one physical table is readable as Delta (Spark) and as Iceberg (Trino). This course writes its Delta tables with UniForm enabled.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — CSV loses the table format entirely: no ACID, no MERGE, no time travel, and slower reads.
- **C** — A second copy is exactly what the team wants to avoid; UniForm needs no copy.
- **D** — Partitioning changes how files are laid out, not which engines can read the table.

references.title: Foundations › File & table formats › The main table formats

questions.question:
Match each ShopFlow need to the file format that fits it best.

| Need | Format |
|---|---|
| Analytics over millions of order rows | [Analytics] |
| Nested events from the website's API | [API events] |
| Write-heavy streaming records with a schema | [Streaming records] |
| A small file a person opens to eyeball | [Small file] |
questions.explanation:
These come from the course's table of common file formats.

- **Analytics → Parquet** — columnar, typed and compressed: the lakehouse default for analytics.
- **API events → JSON** — fits nested, semi-structured data, APIs and events.
- **Streaming records → Avro** — row-based with a schema and compression, made for write-heavy and streaming records.
- **Small file → CSV** — untyped and uncompressed, but fine for tiny data and human eyeballing.

references.title: Foundations › File & table formats › The common file formats

questions.question:
ShopFlow's orders are stored as a Delta table.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.

slots.label: The table's data files are ordinary Parquet files.
Every write appends a new version to the transaction log.
Without a table format, a folder of Parquet files can update a single row atomically.

questions.explanation:
A table format's transaction log is the table's "brain": schema, versions, file list and statistics.

- **Statement 1: Yes** — the data files themselves are just Parquet; the table format adds a log over them.
- **Statement 2: Yes** — each write adds a new version (snapshot) recording the schema and the exact files.
- **Statement 3: No** — a plain folder can't update or delete a single row, or add data atomically.

references.title: Foundations › File & table formats › Table formats — turning files into a table

questions.question:
Match each description to its table format.

| Description | Format |
|---|---|
| A JSON transaction log (`_delta_log`) over Parquet; Databricks-native | [Description 1] |
| Snapshot-based metadata (manifests); engine-agnostic, hidden partitioning | [Description 2] |
| Focused on streaming upserts | [Description 3] |
questions.explanation:
These are the three main table formats.

- **Description 1 → Delta Lake** — Delta keeps a JSON log in `_delta_log` and is Databricks-native.
- **Description 2 → Apache Iceberg** — Iceberg uses snapshots and manifests and is fully engine-agnostic.
- **Description 3 → Apache Hudi** — Hudi is the third option, focused on streaming upserts.

references.title: Foundations › File & table formats › The main table formats

questions.question:
Match each description to its medallion layer.

| Description | Layer |
|---|---|
| An exact, append-only copy of the sources: keep everything | [Raw copy] |
| Cleaned, deduplicated, conformed: the single source of truth | [Clean model] |
| Aggregated marts that answer business questions directly | [Business marts] |
questions.explanation:
Quality and trust rise at each layer, while the data gets smaller and more focused.

- **Raw copy → Bronze** — Bronze keeps everything, even bad or duplicate rows.
- **Clean model → Silver** — Silver is where raw becomes reliable: the single source of truth.
- **Business marts → Gold** — Gold holds small, aggregated, business-ready tables for BI and ML.

references.title: Foundations › Medallion architecture › Bronze — raw
Foundations › Medallion architecture › Silver — clean & conformed
Foundations › Medallion architecture › Gold — business-ready

questions.question:
Months after go-live, you find a bug in ShopFlow's Silver transform. Silver and Gold must be fixed **without** fetching the data from the sources again.

What should you do?

options.text: Restore yesterday's Gold backup
Rebuild Silver and Gold from the raw Bronze tables with the fixed logic
Ask the source teams to resend six months of data
Patch the Gold numbers by hand

questions.explanation:
**Why B is right:** Bronze keeps **everything** so you can always reprocess: if a transform bug is found months later, you rebuild Silver and Gold from Bronze without re-fetching from the source. Bronze is the replay buffer.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — Yesterday's Gold was built with the same bug, and Silver would still be wrong.
- **C** — Re-fetching from the sources is exactly what keeping Bronze avoids.
- **D** — Hand patches can't be traced or repeated, and Silver stays wrong.

references.title: Foundations › Medallion architecture › Bronze — raw
Foundations › Medallion architecture › Why three layers?

questions.question:
ShopFlow is setting up access to its lakehouse layers. Analysts build dashboards, and engineers maintain the transforms.

Which grants follow the medallion guidance?

options.text: Analysts get Gold only; engineers work in Silver; Bronze stays restricted
Analysts get Bronze so they can see all the raw detail
Everyone gets every layer, to keep it simple
Analysts get Silver; Gold is restricted to engineers

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** Access control is one of the benefits of three layers: grant analysts **Gold** only, let engineers work in **Silver**, and keep **Bronze** restricted.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Bronze is raw and untrusted, with duplicates and bad rows, and stays restricted.
- **C** — Giving everyone everything throws away the access-control benefit of the layers.
- **D** — This is backwards: Gold is the layer made for analysts and dashboards.

references.title: Foundations › Medallion architecture › Why three layers?

questions.question:
A new team member is learning ShopFlow's medallion layers.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.

slots.label: Bronze keeps bad and duplicate rows from the sources.
Bronze adds a little ingestion metadata, such as when a row arrived and from which file.
Gold is the single source of truth.

questions.explanation:
Each layer has one job.

- **Statement 1: Yes** — Bronze keeps everything, so you can reprocess later.
- **Statement 2: Yes** — Bronze adds a little ingestion metadata, such as when a row arrived and which file or source it came from.
- **Statement 3: No** — **Silver** is the single source of truth; Gold holds aggregated, business-ready marts built from it.

Foundations › Medallion architecture › Silver — clean & conformed

questions.question:
Updated and late-arriving ShopFlow orders arrive every day. They must replace the earlier versions of those orders in the clean, trusted orders table.

In which layer, and with which operation, is this done?

options.text: In Silver, with MERGE
In Bronze, by deleting the old rows
In Gold, by summing both versions
In the OLTP database, with a report

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** Silver is where updates and late-arriving records are **merged** into the trusted tables, using `MERGE` (a table-format feature).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Bronze is append-only: it keeps everything, including old versions, for reprocessing.
- **C** — Summing both versions would double-count; Gold is built from the already-merged Silver.
- **D** — Analytics doesn't change the source system; the source is what you read from.

references.title: Foundations › Medallion architecture › Silver — clean & conformed

questions.question:
The ShopFlow CEO wants a small, fast table of daily sales, net of returns, for an executive dashboard.

In which layer does this table belong?

options.text: Bronze
Silver
Gold
The staging zone

questions.explanation:
**Why C is right:** **Gold** holds aggregated, purpose-built tables (marts) that answer business questions directly. ShopFlow's `daily_sales` net of returns is one of them.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — Bronze is the raw, append-only copy of the sources.
- **B** — Silver is clean, row-level data (one row per order line), not an aggregated answer.
- **D** — The staging zone holds untouched data as it arrived.

references.title: Foundations › Medallion architecture › Gold — business-ready

questions.question:
ShopFlow applies the medallion layers to its real-time event stream. Match each streaming task to its layer.

| Streaming task | Layer |
|---|---|
| Capture the raw events as they arrive | [Task 1] |
| Clean and sessionise the events | [Task 2] |
| Keep a live orders-per-minute aggregate | [Task 3] |
questions.explanation:
The same three tiers apply to streaming; they just run continuously instead of on a schedule.

- **Task 1 → Bronze** — Bronze captures the raw event stream as it arrives.
- **Task 2 → Silver** — Silver cleans and sessionises the events.
- **Task 3 → Gold** — Gold maintains live aggregates, such as orders per minute or a fraud signal.

references.title: Foundations › Medallion architecture › Medallion works for streaming too

questions.question:
ShopFlow's architects are discussing how strictly to follow the medallion pattern.

Which **two** statements match the course's guidance? (Choose two.)

options.text: Adding a landing zone before Bronze is acceptable
Bronze, Silver and Gold are Databricks' own terms for the pattern
There must always be exactly three layers
Gold should keep a raw copy of every source row
Silver is the layer analysts should query directly

questions.explanation:
**Why A and B are right:** Three layers is a guideline, not a law: teams sometimes add a **landing zone before Bronze** or extra Gold marts. **Medallion (Bronze/Silver/Gold) is Databricks' own term**, recommended on every platform.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **C** — The course says to use as many tiers as the data's messiness justifies, no more and no less.
- **D** — Raw copies belong in Bronze; Gold is small and aggregated.
- **E** — Analysts are granted Gold; engineers work in Silver.

references.title: Foundations › Medallion architecture › Why three layers?
Foundations › Medallion architecture › Concept

questions.question:
ShopFlow is designing its Gold sales mart. The head of sales asks for *"revenue and units sold by product category, by month, for customers in the west region."* Place each column in the table it belongs to.

| Column | Table |
|---|---|
| `line_revenue` | [Box 1] |
| `category` | [Box 2] |
| `region` | [Box 3] |
| `month_name` | [Box 4] |
questions.explanation:
**Numbers go in facts; context goes in dimensions.** The measure you want is in the fact, and every "by …" is a dimension.

- **Box 1 → fact_sales** — revenue is a measure you `SUM`, so it belongs in the fact.
- **Box 2 → dim_product** — category describes the product (what).
- **Box 3 → dim_customer** — region describes the customer (who / where).
- **Box 4 → dim_date** — the month comes from the date dimension (when), computed once.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › The core idea
Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › The two roles, side by side

questions.question:
A ShopFlow analyst joins the `orders` table (one row per order, with `orders.total`) to `order_items` (one row per order line) and sums `orders.total`. Revenue comes out far too high.

What went wrong?

options.text: Two grains were mixed, so each order total was counted once per line
The date dimension is missing
`orders.total` is a semi-additive measure
The dimensions should have been snowflaked

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** This is the **fan-out** trap. Joining a one-row-per-**order** table to a one-row-per-**line** table counts an order-level number once per line. One fact table = one grain; if you need both levels, that's two fact tables.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — A date dimension makes calendar questions easy; it doesn't cause or fix double counting.
- **C** — A total is additive; the problem is that the join repeated it, not how it adds up.
- **D** — Snowflaking dimensions adds joins and doesn't change the grain mix-up.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Grain — decide it first

questions.question:
ShopFlow's fact table has `profit` and `revenue` per order line, and a `margin_pct` column.

What is the correct margin for a whole month?

options.text: `avg(margin_pct)`
`sum(margin_pct)`
`sum(profit) / sum(revenue)`
`max(margin_pct)`

questions.explanation:
**Why C is right:** A percentage is **non-additive**: never sum or average it. Store its parts as additive measures and compute the ratio at query time: `sum(profit) / sum(revenue)`.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — An average of percentages ignores how big each line is; the course says to use `sum(profit) / sum(revenue)`, not `avg(margin_pct)`.
- **B** — Summing percentages produces a meaningless number.
- **D** — The maximum is one line's margin, not the month's.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Measures aren't all equal — additivity

questions.question:
A ShopFlow warehouse table stores `units_on_hand` per product per day. A manager wants one inventory figure for March.

How should you aggregate it?

options.text: Sum the daily values across March
Take the latest value (or an average) across the days, not the sum
Count the number of days
Multiply by the number of products

questions.explanation:
**Why B is right:** Inventory on hand is **semi-additive**: it adds up across some dimensions, but **not across time**. You don't add Monday's stock to Tuesday's; take the latest value or an average.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — Summing daily stock counts the same units again every day.
- **C** — The number of days isn't an inventory figure.
- **D** — Multiplying by products has no meaning for stock on hand.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Measures aren't all equal — additivity

questions.question:
An order line in `fact_sales` refers to a `product_sk` that has no row in `dim_product`. The product report joins them with an `INNER JOIN`.

What happens?

options.text: The query fails with a foreign-key error
The line's revenue lands in a "(null)" category
The line is silently dropped, so product totals come out too low
Trino adds the missing product automatically

questions.explanation:
**Why C is right:** With an `INNER JOIN`, the orphaned line is **silently dropped**: its revenue vanishes from every product report, the totals come out too low, and **nothing errors**.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — Nothing errors; that is what makes orphan keys dangerous.
- **B** — That happens with a `LEFT JOIN`, not an `INNER JOIN`.
- **D** — No engine invents dimension rows; integrity has to be guarded in the pipeline.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Dimensional integrity — and why it's critical

questions.question:
Some ShopFlow order lines arrive with a product key that is missing or unknown. Finance requires that the totals still add up and that the mystery revenue is visible.

What should you do?

options.text: Leave the foreign key NULL
Point those lines at an "Unknown" member in the dimension (e.g. surrogate key -1)
Drop those lines before loading
Use INNER JOINs in every report

questions.explanation:
**Why B is right:** Point missing or unknown keys at a dedicated **Unknown member** (a surrogate key like `-1`, name "Unknown"). Facts never orphan, the total still adds up, and the mystery revenue is visibly attributed to "Unknown" instead of disappearing.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — The course says never to leave a foreign key NULL; reports would show a "(null)" bucket or lose the line.
- **C** — Dropping lines makes the totals too low, which is what finance wants to avoid.
- **D** — An `INNER JOIN` silently drops lines whose key has no dimension row.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Dimensional integrity — and why it's critical

questions.question:
Customer Ada (`customer_id` C-7) lived in Delhi until June 2024 and then moved to Mumbai. `dim_customer` holds two rows for her: `customer_sk` 41 (Delhi, valid to 2024-06-30) and 88 (Mumbai, valid from 2024-07-01). Each sale stores the `customer_sk` that was current at the time of the sale.

Which city does a sale from March 2024 show in "revenue by city"?

options.text: Mumbai, her current city
Delhi, the city she lived in at the time of the sale
Both cities, half each
Neither, because the natural key is C-7

questions.explanation:
**Why B is right:** The March 2024 sale stored `customer_sk = 41`, so it forever joins to **Delhi**. Surrogate keys with SCD Type 2 rows are what make "revenue by the city the customer lived in at the time" possible.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** — Mumbai is row 88, which only sales from July 2024 onwards store.
- **C** — Each sale stores exactly one surrogate key, so it joins to exactly one row.
- **D** — The fact joins on the surrogate key, not the natural key; the natural key alone could hold only one city.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Surrogate keys

questions.question:
Every ShopFlow report re-derives quarters, fiscal periods, weekends and holidays with its own date logic, and the reports disagree on what "Q1" means.

What should you build?

options.text: A date dimension with one row per day and the calendar pre-computed
A second fact table for dates
A Parquet partition for every holiday
A view over the OLTP database

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** A **date dimension** has one row per day with year, quarter, month, weekend and holiday flags computed **once**. Date questions become plain `GROUP BY`s with one shared definition of "Q1", "weekend" and "holiday".

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Dates are context (when), not events with measures, so they belong in a dimension.
- **C** — Partitioning splits files to read less; it doesn't give reports a shared calendar.
- **D** — Analytics belongs off the OLTP system, and a view doesn't pre-compute the calendar.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › The date dimension

questions.question:
Match each query change on ShopFlow's sales star to the OLAP cube operation it performs.

| Query | Operation |
|---|---|
| `WHERE region = 'west'` | [Query 1] |
| `WHERE region IN (…) AND month BETWEEN …` | [Query 2] |
| `GROUP BY category`, from `GROUP BY category, subcategory, product_name` | [Query 3] |
| `GROUP BY year, month, day`, from `GROUP BY year` | [Query 4] |
questions.explanation:
Everyday OLAP verbs are moves on the cube, and each maps to plain SQL.

- **Query 1 → Slice** — fixes one dimension to a single value.
- **Query 2 → Dice** — picks a sub-range on several dimensions.
- **Query 3 → Roll-up** — aggregates **up** the hierarchy, to coarser rows.
- **Query 4 → Drill-down** — goes **down** to finer detail.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Why a dimension table is called a "dimension"
Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Hierarchies

questions.question:
ShopFlow's `dim_product` was split into `dim_product` → `dim_subcategory` → `dim_category`. Analysts now complain that every product report needs extra joins.

Which **two** reasons support flattening it back into a star? (Choose two.)

options.text: Fewer joins and simpler queries
Small, flat dimensions can be broadcast cheaply to every worker
It removes the need for a fact table
Iceberg requires a star schema
It keeps each fact in exactly one place

questions.explanation:
**Why A and B are right:** A **star** keeps each dimension flat (category as a column right on `dim_product`), so queries need **fewer joins**, and small flat dimensions **broadcast** cheaply. Prefer the star unless a dimension is genuinely huge or shared in a way that forces normalization.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **C** — A star always has a fact table at its centre.
- **D** — The course says nothing of the kind; modeling is engine-agnostic.
- **E** — Storing each fact exactly once is the OLTP (normalized) goal, which a star deliberately gives up for read speed.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Hierarchies
Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Why denormalizing into a star pays off

questions.question:
ShopFlow's sales report and returns report disagree on how many customers there are in the west region. Each fact table has its own customer table, built differently.

What should you do?

options.text: Build one conformed `dim_customer` and reuse it for both facts
Add a date dimension
Snowflake both customer tables
Merge the sales and returns facts into one fact table with mixed grains

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** A **conformed dimension** is a single dimension reused by every fact (sales, returns, support), so "customer" means the same thing in every report and the numbers reconcile.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Dates aren't the problem; the two customer definitions are.
- **C** — Snowflaking adds joins; it doesn't make the two definitions agree.
- **D** — Mixing grains in one fact table is the classic bug the course warns against.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Why denormalizing into a star pays off

questions.question:
ShopFlow is reviewing the shape of its fact and dimension tables.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.

slots.label: A fact table is usually tall and narrow: many rows, few columns.
Fact rows are usually updated when a customer moves city.
Dimension tables are usually short and wide: few rows, many descriptive columns.
Dimension tables mostly change through updates, such as a customer moving city.

questions.explanation:
Facts record what happened; dimensions describe the things involved.

- **Statement 1: Yes** — facts hold one row per event, with measures and foreign keys: millions of rows, few columns.
- **Statement 2: No** — facts are immutable records of events: append-only, never edited; the move changes the dimension.
- **Statement 3: Yes** — there are relatively few things but many ways to describe them.
- **Statement 4: Yes** — the lifecycle of a dimension is mostly updates; facts are mostly inserts.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › The two roles, side by side
Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Why a fact table is called a "fact"

questions.question:
Some ShopFlow order lines arrive before the new product they reference has been loaded into `dim_product`.

How should you handle these facts?

options.text: Stage them against the Unknown member, and re-point them once the product row lands
Delete them
Load them with a NULL product key
Stop loading facts until next week

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** For a **late-arriving dimension**, stage the fact against the **Unknown member** and re-point it once the dimension row lands. The general rule is to load dimensions before facts, so a fact never references a row that doesn't exist yet.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Deleting real sales loses revenue from every total.
- **C** — The course says never to leave a foreign key NULL.
- **D** — Holding back all facts delays every report; the Unknown member keeps the pipeline running correctly.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Dimensional integrity — and why it's critical

questions.question:
You wrote a query that counts ShopFlow order lines whose `product_id` has no matching product.

How should the team use it?

options.text: As a data-quality gate in the pipeline: expect 0, and fail the build otherwise
Run it once a year during the audit
Show its result on the CEO's dashboard
Use it to delete the matching products

questions.explanation:
**Why A is right:** An orphan check should return **0**. Wire it into the pipeline as a data-quality gate, so a broken key **fails the build** instead of silently skewing a dashboard.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** — Once a year is far too late: a broken key quietly skews every report in between.
- **C** — The check guards the data before it reaches dashboards; executives don't need its count.
- **D** — The orphans are order lines with no product; there are no matching products to delete.

references.title: Foundations › Dimensional modeling (facts & dimensions) › Dimensional integrity — and why it's critical
